summary: Describes problems with flow-based measurement, such as scalability, flexibility and export reliability, and shows how IPFIX Mediation may help. It gives examples of where mediation applies. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Network equipment can produce more traffic records than one collector can handle, and different users need different views of the data. RFC 5982 describes an intermediate processor that can transform, combine, and distribute those records.

questions: what can an ipfix mediator do
subtitle: How an intermediary can transform flow records to meet measurement and export needs.

tldr.problem: Flow-measurement systems must handle growing traffic, different application needs, and equipment with different capabilities and export formats.
tldr.mechanism: An IPFIX Mediator receives record streams and applies intermediate processing such as aggregation, correlation, filtering, anonymization, or conversion before export.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes mediation use cases and implementation problems, including preserving exporter, timing, template, and topology information. It is Informational and defines no complete mediation standard.

today: RFC 5982 is an Informational RFC published in August 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it describes the IPFIX Mediation problem space and implementation considerations.

sections.title: What IPFIX Mediation Adds
sections.content:
Flow-based measurement summarizes traffic seen at observation points. An IPFIX Mediator is an IPFIX device that receives record streams, applies one or more intermediate processes, and exports the transformed records. The process may be hosted in a separate mediator or in an original exporter.

The input can come from IPFIX collectors, metering processes, files, other mediators, or other data sources. The RFC also describes converting data from another format, such as NetFlow version 9, before exporting it with IPFIX. It presents a generalized intermediate-device concept rather than a new packet-measurement protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A mediator receives traffic records, changes them as needed, then sends the resulting records to another system. It can help connect equipment and collectors that have different limits or needs.

sections.title: Why Measurement Systems Need Mediation
sections.content:
Traffic growth can produce more flow records than a single collector can process. Reducing data at the exporter through sampling, filtering, or aggregation can lower the load, but it may remove detail needed to detect subtle changes or investigate anomalies.

Different applications also need different record detail, and an exporter may lack the resources to perform several complex metering tasks at once. Networks often combine devices from different vendors, software versions, and generations, with different metering abilities and data formats. The RFC presents mediation as a way to move processing between exporters and collectors while adapting records to these varied conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: One system may not be able to collect every record or prepare every view users need. Reducing the data too early can hide useful details, so processing can be moved to an intermediate point.

sections.title: Ways a Mediator Can Process Records
sections.content:
The RFC describes several uses for intermediate processing. A mediator can change flow granularity by grouping records with different flow keys, correlate records from multiple observation points, combine consecutive records over time, or combine records from multiple locations. It can also anonymize records before sharing them across administrative boundaries.

Other examples include aggregating data at a branch office to reduce the amount sent over a limited link, distributing record types to different collectors, sampling or filtering records, and converting legacy export protocols to IPFIX. The RFC describes these as applicability examples; the exact processing depends on the measurement purpose and the available data.
sections.plainLanguage: A mediator can group records by a different key, combine observations across time or locations, remove identifying details, or route records to different collectors. The right operation depends on what the measurements are meant to show.

sections.title: Information a Mediator Must Preserve
sections.content:
Mediation can make records harder to interpret if the mediator loses information. A collector may need to know which original exporter produced a record, what reference time applies to delta timestamps, and how incoming template identifiers relate to outgoing identifiers. Options Template information, such as sampling rates, may also be needed to interpret the measurements correctly.

Aggregation must account for network topology to avoid double counting. The mediator may also need to report which transformation it performed and how non-key fields were handled when records with different values were combined. The RFC identifies these as implementation issues that require clear handling between original exporters, mediators, and collectors.
sections.plainLanguage: A mediator must keep enough context for the collector to understand where records came from and what they mean. If it combines records, it must account for the network layout and explain how the values were combined.

sections.title: Open Issues and Security
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that mediation can help administrators choose among different processing functions, but standards for mediation were not yet established. Open issues include what information must pass between original exporters and collectors, how transport sessions map through mediators, and which internal components a mediator needs.

Measurement systems must protect confidential traffic data, prevent incorrect data injection and unauthorized access, and consider attacks on the mediator itself. A mediator can also expose end-user details when it combines fine-grained measurements or serves multiple customers. The RFC discusses anonymization, aggregation, access controls, and protected transport as relevant safeguards.
sections.plainLanguage: Collectors need consistent information about what a mediator changed and which exporter supplied the data. Mediators also need protection because they can see sensitive traffic records for several users or customers.
